text: Because the spacecraft was a contamination risk. Cassini had spent years drifting around Saturn, and all that travel means it could be carrying bits of Earth life. The issue is that moons like Enceladus or Titan might have liquid water and could host life. So rather than leave the spacecraft in a random orbit where it might hit one of those moons and bring microbes, the mission planners aimed it to plunge into Saturn's atmosphere and burn up. If it was going to hit a moon, they could choose a less interesting target. It's a way of keeping the search for alien life clean.

Most of the time, the leg that stays on the board is getting loaded every time you push. You're standing with your full weight on one ankle, knee and hip while the other leg does the work. That sounds harmless, but skateboards are not a flat floor. The board rolls, tilts, catches small cracks, and every push changes where your weight sits. Your stationary leg is doing fine work, stabilizing the board, absorbing small shocks, and keeping you from falling. If that side starts to ache, the usual cause is simple overload. You may be pushing from a weak or poorly aligned leg, or you may be using the wrong leg as the pusher and leaving the other one to hold everything.

I'd check your stance first. If your stationary leg is bent or twisted at the ankle, the pain can move into the knee or hip. Skate shoes with stiff soles can make that worse. I'd also look at how you push. A short, low push with a steady, slightly bent stationary leg is much easier on the joint than a high, forceful kick. If the pain is in the ankle, it may be from repeated impact and poor balance. If it's in the knee or hip, think about alignment and how much time you're riding.

Sometimes the board itself is the problem. A deck that's too flexy or wheels that catch can make the stationary leg work harder. Worn bearings can make the board wander, and your body compensates with the planted leg.

The fix is not dramatic. Change which leg pushes if you always use the same side. Keep the planted leg straight but not locked, keep your weight centered, and push in short bursts. If it keeps hurting, reduce the time you spend on the board.

The label is about where a family’s ancestors came from, not where a person was born. For most Black Americans, that ancestry runs back to West and Central Africa, brought over through the transatlantic slave trade. Some people have Caribbean or Brazilian roots too, so the name does not fit everyone neatly. “Afro-American” is the older, less common form; most people just say African American. That says there is an African connection in the bloodline, not that the person grew up in Africa. It is similar to saying someone is Italian American or Irish American. You do not have to be born in Italy to carry that background. In practice, many Black Americans identify with the broader African descent, even if their immediate family has lived in the US for generations. The word is a rough shorthand, and not every person will feel it fits perfectly.

Mostly it comes in from the sides, not from the sky. Trucks cross from Lebanon and Iraq, and some shipments are said to arrive with Iranian help. Locally, guns show up at back-room dealers and in ruined army depots. People keep buying them because the guns are still useful for holding a street, a checkpoint, or a neighborhood. Militias and local leaders still need them, and ordinary families buy them for protection. The state is weak in parts, so a rifle or an AK can matter more than a paper document. If you lose your gun, you can be pushed out of your own area.

I think the core problem is that the same brain systems that make something feel amazing are also the ones your body starts counting on. When a drug pushes those systems hard, the brain adjusts its own baseline, and what used to feel like ordinary life starts feeling dull by comparison. That is tolerance. You need more for the same feeling, and if you stop, the body resists the sudden drop. Withdrawal is the price of the reset.

The reason people ask this is that we imagine a magic pill that gives the high and leaves everything else alone. In practice, a drug has to get into the brain and change how the reward circuitry behaves. If it changes pleasure strongly, it will also change how the body handles stress, sleep, appetite, heart rate, hormones and mood. You cannot easily separate the euphoria from the side effects because they are both the body reacting to the same chemical event.

I would be less surprised by a drug with mild effects. A drug that gives intense euphoria with zero adverse effects would have to dodge tolerance, dependence, withdrawal and the weird everyday stuff like dizziness, sweating or a racing pulse. I guess the reward system is not a clean switch. It is a network, and the more violently you pull on it, the more the rest of the body notices.

A lot of the fear around drugs comes from seeing the worst cases, the overdose, the crash after the high, the next day when your head feels like it has been shaken. Those things happen when the dose is high or the person pushes past what their body can handle. Some drugs are more forgiving, but the question is about intense pleasure. That usually means the effect is strong enough to disturb normal function.

There are medicines that act on the same systems and have a smaller blast radius. They are not zero effect, just less. And even those can build dependence if the brain gets used to them. The brain adapts, and adaptation is not always bad, but it means the original dose no longer does the same thing.

The word bad is a little too broad. Some drugs can help, like antibiotics or painkillers. But when you want a strong pleasure hit, you are asking the body to do something it was not designed to do for hours. The nervous system is not built to stay at peak pleasure without consequences. It wants a return to normal.

Hi,

The pain isn't just in your head. On a long shopping day your body is doing more than standing around, walking a lot, stopping and starting, carrying bags, adjusting to crowds and noise. That kind of low-level strain can hurt in the feet, knees, back or neck. If you're also thinking about what she'll ask you to try on or buy, the tension can make the aches worse.

I'd check your shoes first. A pair that looks fine on the shelf can still be the cause if the soles have gone flat or the fit has changed.

Hi,

That sounds like a little word-priming trick your brother is using. You were repeating and spelling silk, which makes the similar-sounding word milk easier to retrieve. Cows are also strongly linked to milk, so when he asked what they drink, the familiar association jumped out before the boring fact, water. It is not that you forgot what cows drink. Your mind was stuck on the last words you had just been forced to say, and your brother took advantage of that. The spell-out part makes it worse, because you have to process the letters of silk, which keeps milk right at the edge of attention. Do not worry about being the only one to slip up. Many people say milk when caught in that loop. If you want to break it, pause before answering. Next time, count slowly to three before you answer, and say the correct answer, water.

Thanks

Hi,

I only saw the subject line, so I'll keep this practical. The first thing is to pin down what you can actually borrow. Get pre-approval from a lender, not just a quote. That tells you a real ceiling and stops you falling in love with a house you cannot pay for. If you send the actual questions, I can go through them one by one.

Once you have that, walk into viewings with a short list of non-negotiables, like commute, storage, light, and whether the bones are sound. Do not let a shiny kitchen override a bad location or a damp wall. Ask the seller or agent for service records, planning documents, and any known defects. For an older home, budget for a proper structural and damp survey, and for a newer one, check the warranties and utility bills before you commit.

I'd be more worried about hidden problems than about the sticker price. A small repair now can become a big bill later. Negotiate from the survey, not from a feeling. And if you are worried about the neighborhood, go at different times, including evening and weekend, and talk to people at the shop or the pub.

Thanks

Hi,

The difference is mostly in the formula, not the bottle. A 3-in-1 bodywash/shampoo/conditioner tries to be mild enough for skin and still clean enough for hair, so it uses a softer surfactant mix, some conditioning polymers, and moisturizing ingredients that can work on both. The individual counterparts are usually optimized for one job, while the combo is a compromise that has to be safe and effective across skin and hair. A plain bodywash is built for skin, so it may have a different lather and more skin-friendly additives. A plain shampoo is built for hair, and a conditioner is built to coat and soften hair. The 3-in-1 sits between those, trying to do all three jobs without needing three products.

A 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner only covers hair, cleaning and conditioning in one step. The 3-in-1 adds body to that mix. In practice, the 3-in-1 usually feels gentler on skin and is meant to rinse clean from both places. You might notice it leaves hair feeling less dry than plain shampoo, and leaves skin feeling less tight than plain bodywash. I would not expect it to replace specialized products for every need, but for everyday use it can save a shelf.

Thanks

Hi,

They use fixed GPS markers on bedrock and satellites to pin their positions very precisely. You can’t watch a continent slide like a rock on a table, so the markers have to stay put. By comparing their positions every year, you get a speed in centimeters per year.

The satellites have to be tracked against a stable reference, and the ground stations have to remain stable. A station that moves with the crust gives the real movement. One on a cracked foundation or near traffic can make the numbers look messy. Even a small foundation shift can change the numbers quite a bit. The measurements are small, a few centimeters, so the error has to be tiny. That’s why they use many stations, repeat observations, and careful surveying.

One thing people miss is that a continent isn’t moving in one direction like a car. Different spots on it can drift differently, and sometimes a coast speeds up or slows down. So the answer isn’t a single speed for the whole plate. It’s a pattern from lots of points.

In practice, they also use old survey marks and modern GPS together, so the record doesn’t just jump when the technology changes.

Thanks

When two relatives have a child, the child is more likely to inherit the same rare variant from both sides of the family. Most harmful genes are recessive, so they can hide for generations in people who carry one copy without showing signs. Inbreeding raises the chance that a child ends up with two copies. If those copies affect the brain, that can make the difference between normal development and lower cognitive scores.

It is not that close relatives have worse genes. The parents may be healthy but the child can receive matching harmful variants. The brain is sensitive to these changes during early development, so the effect often shows up as lower IQ rather than one specific disease. The closer the relationship, the greater the risk. In practice, this generally means inbred offspring are statistically much more likely to fall below average. Not every single child will be affected.

Your arm is thick with muscle and sits under loose skin, so a hit, shot or knife often lands in tissue that can absorb the blow. The nerves there are not as tightly packed as in the face, hands, ribs or spine. Adrenaline can also dull the pain, and the arm is far enough from the core that the injury feels less urgent to the brain. That does not mean it is painless. A deep wound or one near a nerve can still hurt badly. I’d be more worried if the injury is in the shoulder or upper arm, because the main nerve bundle and big vessels are close. For a new colleague, the key thing is that location, tissue type and stress response make the same kind of injury feel different in different places.

A bruise or small cut feels less scary, less urgent and still needs a check.

CO is dangerous because it quietly takes the place of oxygen inside red blood cells. The gas has almost no smell or color, so you might not notice it. It is often made when fuels burn without enough air, like a stove, boiler, or car engine. In the blood, oxygen normally binds to hemoglobin and carries it to tissues. CO grabs the same spot much more strongly than oxygen. Its grip on hemoglobin is roughly two hundred times stronger than oxygen's. Once it attaches, the cell cannot carry oxygen as well, and the tissues get short on oxygen even if the air has plenty of it. That is why people feel confused, dizzy, or sick before they understand what is happening.

The body deals with CO2 in a different way. CO2 is the normal waste product of breathing. It is far more soluble in blood than CO, and the lungs remove it efficiently. Most of it travels to tissues as bicarbonate, and only a small part needs to bind to hemoglobin. That means a normal amount of CO2 in the air is something the body expects and can clear. High CO2 can still make you feel bad and at very high levels it can be dangerous, but under everyday conditions it does not quietly replace oxygen in the same way.

The practical point is that CO can hide in a room, and by the time symptoms show up, oxygen delivery has already been reduced. Because you cannot smell it, a CO alarm is useful in rooms with combustion equipment. For a workplace wiki, the key thing to remember is that the danger is not simply that CO is a gas, it is that it binds so tightly to hemoglobin that oxygen transport falls off. That is the difference from CO2, which is handled as ordinary metabolic waste.

In an aircraft emergency, the brace position is a way of getting your body ready for a sudden jolt. You put your feet on the floor, lean toward the seat or a surface in front of you, and hold your hands near your chest or head. The point is to stop your body from moving forward and hitting the seat, tray table, or other people. When the aircraft stops or drops quickly, everything inside keeps moving. Your muscles and bones take the hit better if they are braced and aligned with the direction of force.

For a new colleague, the key idea is simple: do not flail or sit loose. Keep your back against the seat, bend your knees slightly if possible, and hold the position until the aircraft is secure. In a row seat, keep your head near the backrest, not thrown into the front. This reduces the chance of a hard collision with the structure ahead of you. It is not a guaranteed safety measure, and it will not save everyone from every accident. But it is one of the few things a passenger can do that may reduce the force on your neck, spine, and internal organs during a hard landing or crash.

Some very old trading houses and family workshops did exist before the industrial era, but they were usually local or regional. A blacksmith's shop, a monastery brewery, or a merchant's warehouse did not have a global brand. Production was small, trade routes were slow, and advertising was rare, so names rarely became familiar outside their town.

The industrial era changed that. Factories, railways, telegraph lines, and mass media let companies reach many customers at once across countries. That is why the household names you know by name mostly grew as brands after industrialisation, even if their roots go further back.

I stopped believing the sticker rate on a car loan the first time the total came out higher than my bank quote. I walked into the lot with a printed bank offer in my pocket. It was 4.25% for 72 months, with a modest fee. The dealer salesman slid a paper in front of me with 2.99% and said it was the best deal in the country. It looked like magic, but the magic was in the line items he did not point to.

The dealer quoted a lower interest rate, yes, but the loan amount was bigger. He had put in a $450 doc fee, a $600 protection package, $2,300 in floor mats, spray-in bedliner, and a set of wheel covers that I did not ask for. The low rate applied to a bigger number. The bank quote was higher, 4.25%, but it was for exactly the vehicle price I wanted, no bundled extras, no pressure to add products. The bank also gave me the option to pick my own term, so I could stretch the loan if my monthly payment was too high. The bank fee was $950. That stung, but I knew the exact borrowing amount and could compare it against the dealer's inflated balance. It was a small price for keeping the loan simple.

I have a theory about this. The low dealer rate is not really the point. It is a way to get you into the showroom and into the payment conversation. Once you are there, the total payment is rebuilt around extras and fees, and the low rate no longer protects you. You can get a lower nominal rate and still pay more because the loan balance is inflated. The bank charges a fee too, but it is disclosed and usually smaller than the stack of add-ons a dealer can put in front of you.

I would rather pay a little more interest at the bank and keep the loan clean. A lower rate at the lot can still end up as a bigger bill when you add the extras. Before I sign anything, I write down the total cost. Loan amount, monthly payment, number of payments, fees, and any add-ons. That is the number I compare, not the rate on the top line. The dealer can make the rate look beautiful while the total quietly grows. I have seen it enough to trust the bank's simple math more.

I'd rather have one clear rule than fifty different ones. That's my take on marijuana legality across the states. It's nice that states got to decide, but the patchwork leaves people guessing. If you drive across a state line with a small bag of buds in your glove box, what's legal there may not be here. I'd be more worried about that than about the price on the shelf. A shop can sell in one town and not the next, and a patient's doctor can say one thing while the state pharmacy says another.

States moving first made sense, and I don't think that was a mistake. But the long run needs something simpler. I guess a national standard would be easier to live with.

I think about tiny electrical events in my heart. It is not like a battery sitting in my chest. My cells make their own little voltage differences. Sodium and potassium are not evenly spread across the cell membrane. When the membrane opens certain gates, ions rush in or out, and that movement is the current. In a nerve, a small depolarisation triggers more gates to open, so the signal travels down the fibre. My heart does the same thing, and a heartbeat shows on an ECG. The body does not produce electricity. It stores charge and releases it in bursts.

The most useful thing about sampling an old record is not finding the right song, it is finding the right two bars. I've watched producers sit in front of a DAW with a 1970s breakbeat pulled off an old LP, and all they want is the part where the drums get loose. They loop that section, strip the rest, maybe drop the pitch a half step, and build new drums around it. The old track becomes a floor to play on. That floor is where the new song starts to live. I have spent a lot of time trying to find the exact second where the room moves, and that is the part I care about most.

A lot of the work is listening for texture. I've seen this done with a dusty 45, with a vinyl rip, or with a CD file. The source doesn't matter much once you have the right fragment. A vocal phrase, a horn stab, a bass line that feels like it is leaning forward. You can hear a sample working even before you understand what the producer is doing to it. Sometimes it is just a drum break, sometimes it is a whole section. The difference matters. A loop repeats and becomes the track's pulse. A one-off hit lands once and gives a moment of color. I think the best samples choose the smaller option, the one phrase, because it leaves room for the new arrangement. If you take too much of the old song, you have to fight the original composition.

There is also the rights side, which people often forget. The person sampling usually needs permission from the copyright holder, which is normally the label, and sometimes a publisher if a melody or lyrics are in there. A producer can cut the sample and keep it in the mix, but before release there is a clearing step. You ask for permission and pay for it. Some tracks go out with uncleared samples and wait to see what happens. That is a gamble, and it is why a lot of producers would rather pay a few dollars to be safe. I would be more worried about the rights side than the sound side.

The thing I like is that sampling is not just copying. It is choosing a piece of someone else's past and making it do a new job. The old song stops being only an old song and becomes part of a new one.

Mine started with a tight band around my temples, then the whole top of my head felt squeezed. I had been staring at a screen for hours, and the room was stuffy and my water bottle was still half full. I took a break, opened a window, drank the water, and the pain eased. That’s the part I find hard to explain to other people: for me, it’s not just a bad day. My head hurts because I keep pushing through little signals—dry eyes, shallow breathing, skipping lunch, a neck held too far back. The pain is like a warning that my body is running on fumes. I’ve learned to stop earlier. A short walk, a glass of water, and five minutes of slow breathing usually stop it before it becomes that awful pounding under my eyes. Sometimes I still ignore it, and pay for it by late night.

I can't even tell you if the food is good, because we never got to eat. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday. We picked this place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and thought it would be easy. We put our names into their completely useless digital waitlist and were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, but then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually mentioned we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15. It was just a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait extends that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn't wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if it were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly there was no line at all. For two people it came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

Four stars, and I'm keeping it. The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had pulled off a keycap and found out for myself, brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That really mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar closer to the middle now.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, though the under-21 side of it, so I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and it was mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

The circular stage is genuinely smart. You look down into it, so from almost any seat you get a decent view, which is rare in Vegas. Some of the individual acts are impressive too, the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not exactly a rip-off, but if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats, and this one had maybe less clarity.

Clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. A dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like pretty images thrown at you, and the show never says what it’s trying to say. Way too much is happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would have hit harder. It felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

If you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps a little. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t really think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by phone. They never showed up, because the sales rep wrote the delivery address down wrong. Her handwritten 7 was read as a 1. The address was supposed to be 5407, but the package went to 5401. The people at 5401 took it to the local UPS store for return. Then the package disappeared and was never seen or heard from again. We didn't find out about it for several weeks. During the dispute, we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount wouldn't refund the original two. The owner handled it at that point. He admitted the shipment went to the wrong address but said no refund until the shirts were returned. He claimed we were partly to blame because we had not been friendly enough to the people at 5401, four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company and eventually got a credit.
